newsitem.title: USA: Emerging market debts slide with U.S. Treasuries.
newsitem.headline: Emerging market debts slide with U.S. Treasuries.

text.p: Emerging market debts began the new year on a downbeat but managed to outperform U.S. Treasuries in moderate trading on Thursday, traders said.
The ability of major Brady bonds to withstand the pressure of sinking Treasuries was a good sign, they said, although volume was unimpressive.

The bellwether Brazil C bonds and Argentina FRB had hardly budged since December 20 -- a period over which the U.S. long bond yield rose from 6.60 to 6.75 percent, said Marcelo Fleury, head of Brazil desk at Garban Corp.
Brazil C slipped 3/8 to 73-1/4 bid and Argentina FRBs was off 5/8 at 86-3/8 bid.
"Brady investors have stayed on the sidelines," he said. Turnover, though still thin, was six times Monday's level, he estimated.

James Barrineau, emerging market fixed income strategist at Smith Barney, attributed the mild selloff to "periodic bumps" in the market, with no dumping or frantic flight to quality. But he said he expects volatility for the emerging market debts in 1997 after the big gains achieved in 1996.
Among the Latin Bradies, Barrineau said Venezuela papers could face turbulence because the government might let the bolivar weaken as it bites the bullet and lays off workers.
Mexico's midterm congressional and local elections in 1997 began casting shadows as potential political unrest could bring volatility to financial markets, he noted.
Mexico Pars fell 7/8 to 72-3/8 bid and Mexico UMS-26 lost 1-1/8 to 104-1/2 bid.
Among the major Bradies, Brazil was the least affected by the weak U.S. Treasuries. Brazil new money bond in fact gained 1-1/8 to 81-1/2 bid.
Garban's Fleury said that moves in the "New Money" bond were exaggerated by its illiquidity, adding that the bond tended to move "EI" bond, which gained 1/8 to 87-1/5.
Peru's "when-issued" debt papers did not move as the hostage crisis entered its 16th day. Peru Citi was bid 116 even.
"The current crisis will blow over," said Barrineau at Smith Barney. "Investors are taking it in stride."
After climbing almost 60 percent in 1996, Peru's debt looked fairly rich to some investors, but to others it has more room as the restructuring exchange takes place as expected this year, he said.
